sources.note: Treats a transformer forward pass as a controlled dynamical system with depth as time, lifts it with the Koopman operator to get a finite linear realisation whose spectrum is coordinate-free, proves that spectrum is recoverable from finite calibration data at the parametric rate, and then proves that the identifiable object and the human-legible object cannot be the same object.
sources.title: Intrinsic Structure: Spectral Identifiability for Mechanistic Interpretability

sources.note: Fits a post-hoc sparse autoencoder to the frozen dense tensors that two vision-language agents exchange, finds a 128-fold payload reduction at near-identical reconstruction and roughly unchanged single-run accuracy, and then spends most of the paper enumerating the alternative explanations its own design cannot rule out.
sources.title: Post-Hoc Sparse Coding of Latent Communication Between Vision-Language Model Agents

sources.note: Trains sparse autoencoders on language model activations to recover an overcomplete dictionary of sparsely activating directions, and shows those directions are more interpretable and more precisely causal than neurons, PCA or ICA.
sources.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models

result.definition: Learning an overcomplete set of directions in which activations are represented by a few active coefficients, on the hypothesis that this takes features out of superposition. The foundational source establishes the case: a single-hidden-layer autoencoder with tied weights and an L1 penalty, trained unsupervised on activations at orders of magnitude less compute than the model itself, yields directions that score higher on automated interpretability than PCA, ICA, the neuron basis and random directions, and that localise behaviour more tightly -- fewer feature patches reach a given KL divergence from a counterfactual target, at smaller edit magnitude. The other two sources bound it from opposite directions. One proves the non-identifiability is structural, since the reconstruction-and-sparsity objective does not enforce the invariance identifiability requires, and shows that adding the missing term improves identifiability 41 percent while degrading reconstruction, live-feature count and cross-seed agreement -- leaving open whether a dictionary can be sparse, reconstructive and invariant at once. The other supplies a caution about reading the output at all: a fitted dictionary using 50 of 4096 features is equally consistent with low-rank input structure or optimisation collapse, and that paper names the matched-rate baselines that would separate them as not run. The archive's position is therefore that sparse dictionaries beat the alternatives on interpretability scores and that a feature count is not a vocabulary until the cheaper explanations have been excluded.
